meta.title: Inferno Tactical Map
meta.text: Dante Alighieri, Inferno (c. 1308–1321). Italian text and H. W. Longfellow translation (1867), both public domain.
meta.scale: The globe follows the medieval picture: Hell is a cone under Jerusalem whose point is the center of the Earth, and Mount Purgatory rises from the ocean on the opposite side. Dante gives sequence, direction and a few measurements; vertical depths and ring widths here are interpretive, loosely following the Renaissance reconstructions of Manetti and Galileo (1588).

measures.text: The ninth bolgia is twenty-two miles around.
The tenth bolgia is eleven miles around and no less than half a mile across.
Nimrod's face is as long and wide as the bronze pinecone of St. Peter's in Rome.

path.label: Climbs toward the hill; the three beasts
Gate of Dis shut against them
The Heavenly Messenger opens the gate
Pope Anastasius' tomb; Virgil maps Hell
Nessus carries Dante across the ford
The waterfall; the cord is thrown
A horn blast; towers that are giants

nodes.note: Dante is 35, “midway” through a 70-year life, on the night before Good Friday, 1300.
nodes.it: Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita / mi ritrovai per una selva oscura, / ché la diritta via era smarrita.
nodes.en: Midway upon the journey of our life / I found myself within a forest dark, / For the straightforward pathway had been lost.

nodes.note: A hill whose shoulders are lit by the planet that leads everyone right: the sun. Dante tries to climb it directly and fails.
Light, quick, spotted. Often read as fraud or lust. Dante will later throw his cord to Geryon, the cord he once hoped to catch this beast with.
Head high, raging hunger. Often read as pride or violence.
Lean and full of cravings; she drives Dante back down into the dark. Usually read as greed. Virgil prophesies a Greyhound (veltro) will hunt her down (I.101-111).
The Roman poet appears, hoarse from long silence, and becomes Dante's guide.
nodes.it: chi per lungo silenzio parea fioco.

nodes.note: Virgil explains he was sent: Mary, through St. Lucy, moved Beatrice, who came down to Limbo to ask him to guide Dante.
Virgil says the hemisphere they left is centered on where the sinless man was killed. Commentators place Hell's funnel directly beneath Jerusalem.
The inscription speaks in the gate's own voice. Virgil later notes this outer gate stands without a lock since Christ broke it (VIII.124-126).
nodes.it: Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate.
nodes.en: All hope abandon, ye who enter in!

nodes.sin: Never committed to good or evil
nodes.note: They chase a whirling banner forever, stung by wasps and hornets; worms drink their blood and tears. Heaven and Hell both reject them.
Angels who neither rebelled with Lucifer nor stayed loyal to God.
“Him who made through cowardice the great refusal.” Unnamed; most often identified as Pope Celestine V, who resigned in 1294 and opened the way for Boniface VIII.
The first of Hell's rivers. All four are fed by the tears of the Old Man of Crete (XIV.112-120).
The ferryman with wheels of flame around his eyes. He refuses a living man until Virgil silences him.
nodes.it: Caron dimonio, con occhi di bragia

nodes.note: The ground shakes, a red light flashes, and Dante falls “like a man whom sleep has seized.” How he crosses is never told.

No weeping, only sighs. Infants, women and men who were good but unbaptized: “they sinned not” (IV.34), yet merit is not enough without baptism. Virgil says he is one of them (IV.39). Their whole punishment is absence.
nodes.it: semo perduti, e sol di tanto offesi / che sanza speme vivemo in disio.
nodes.en: Lost are we and are only so far punished, / That without hope we live on in desire.

nodes.note: Virgil remembers “a Mighty One, crowned with sign of victory” who took Adam, Abel, Noah, Moses, Abraham, David, Rachel and others out of Limbo. The earthquake at that moment broke Hell's rock: see the landslide (XII) and the broken bridges (XXI, XXIII).
The great poets welcome Dante as the sixth among them.
nodes.it: sì ch'io fui sesto tra cotanto senno.
nodes.en: So that the sixth was I, ’mid so much wit.

nodes.note: Seven high walls, a moat, seven gates, a green meadow inside, lit by its own light.
Heroes of Troy and Rome: Camilla, Penthesilea, King Latinus and Lavinia, Brutus who drove out Tarquin, Lucretia, Julia, Marcia, Cornelia, and Saladin “alone, apart.”
“The master of those who know,” surrounded by Socrates, Plato, Democritus, Diogenes, Heraclitus, Cicero, Seneca, Euclid, Ptolemy, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna and Averroës.
nodes.it: vidi 'l maestro di color che sanno

nodes.note: Hell's judge. He wraps his tail around himself as many times as the circle a soul must go down to.
nodes.it: cignesi con la coda tante volte / quantunque gradi vuol che giù sia messa.

nodes.note: Lovers who let desire rule reason are blown forever like starlings in winter.
nodes.it: La bufera infernal, che mai non resta

nodes.note: Virgil names the line of famous lovers: Semiramis, Dido (who broke faith with Sychaeus's ashes), Cleopatra, Helen.
“The great Achilles, who fought with love at the end.”
Killed with Paolo, her husband's brother, after reading of Lancelot and Guinevere together. Her husband Gianciotto is bound for Caina.
nodes.it: Amor, ch'a nullo amato amar perdona,
nodes.en: Love, that exempts no one beloved from loving,

nodes.note: Never speaks. He weeps while Francesca tells their story; Dante faints from pity.
nodes.it: quel giorno più non vi leggemmo avante.
nodes.en: That day no farther did we read therein.

nodes.note: Three throats, red eyes, greasy black beard. Virgil silences him by throwing fistfuls of dirt into his mouths.
Eternal, cursed, cold, heavy rain, hail and dirty snow; the ground stinks.
A Florentine glutton (“Hog”). He prophesies Florence's civil strife, then tells Dante that Farinata, Tegghiaio, Rusticucci, Arrigo and Mosca are “among the blacker souls” further down.
God of wealth, a “cursed wolf.” He collapses like a sail when its mast snaps.
nodes.it: Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe!

nodes.note: Two half-circles roll great weights with their chests, crash, and shout “Why do you hoard?” “Why do you waste?” then turn and do it again.
Clergy, popes and cardinals, “in whom avarice does its worst.” None are recognizable.
Virgil explains Fortune as a heavenly minister who turns worldly goods from people to people.
The wrathful fight naked in the mud; the sullen lie under it, gurgling a hymn they cannot say whole.
“Sullen we were in the sweet air.” Their sighs make bubbles on the surface.
Two small flames on top answered by a third far off: a warning to Dis that someone is coming.
The boatman. His boat sits low in the water only once Dante, who has weight, steps in.
A Florentine of the Adimari family rises from the mud and grabs at the boat. The other wrathful tear him apart; he bites himself.
Iron-looking walls; its “mosques” glow red from the eternal fire inside. Lower Hell begins here.
More than a thousand rained from heaven. They slam the gate in Virgil's face; he recalls they tried the same at the outer gate when Christ came.
Megaera, Alecto, Tisiphone, bloodstained with green hydras for hair, call for Medusa. Virgil covers Dante's eyes.
nodes.it: Vegna Medusa: sì 'l farem di smalto

nodes.note: Crosses the Styx with dry feet. The damned scatter like frogs before a snake. He opens the gate with a small wand.
A plain of open sarcophagi, heated hotter than iron in a forge. Lids will be sealed after Judgment Day (X.10-12).
Ghibelline leader who saved Florence from destruction after Montaperti. He prophesies Dante's exile (X.79-81).
nodes.it: Vedi là Farinata che s'è dritto: / da la cintola in sù tutto 'l vedrai.

nodes.note: Rises beside Farinata asking about his son, Dante's friend the poet Guido Cavalcanti. Dante hesitates and he sinks back, thinking Guido dead.
Farinata names more than a thousand in his tomb, including Frederick II and Cardinal Ottaviano degli Ubaldini.
They shelter behind it from the stench and pause to let their noses adjust.
The poem's own legend: violence (Circle 7, three rings), simple fraud (Circle 8), and treachery (Circle 9), following Aristotle's ethics.
A ruin like the rockslide south of Trent. Virgil explains it fell in the earthquake when Christ harrowed Hell.
“The infamy of Crete” sprawls on the broken edge and bites itself in rage; they slip past while he thrashes.
Boiling blood; souls are sunk as deep as their violence. Named Phlegethon at XIV.131-135.
Thousands of centaurs patrol with bows. Chiron, Achilles' teacher, notices Dante moves the stones he touches: he is alive.
Sunk to the eyebrows. Ezzelino da Romano (dark hair) and Obizzo d'Este (blond), killed by his stepson.
Standing apart: he murdered Henry of Almain in a church at Viterbo.
Where the river is shallowest, along with highwaymen Rinier da Corneto and Rinier Pazzo.
Bird bodies, human faces, wide wings. They nest in the trees and feed on the leaves, which hurts the souls inside.
Frederick II's chancellor, disgraced by envious courtiers, killed himself. Dante snaps a twig and it bleeds and speaks.
nodes.it: Uomini fummo, e or siam fatti sterpi:
nodes.en: Men once we were, and now are changed to trees;

nodes.note: Violent wasters of their own property, chased and torn apart by black hounds.
A bush torn by the hunt. He hanged himself in his own house.
nodes.it: Io fei gibetto a me de le mie case.

nodes.note: Broad flakes of fire fall slowly like snow in the Alps on windless days. Blasphemers lie face up; usurers sit; sodomites keep moving.
One of the Seven against Thebes, struck by Jove's lightning. Still defiant; Virgil says his rage is his punishment.
nodes.it: Qual io fui vivo, tal son morto.
nodes.en: Such as I was living, am I, dead.

nodes.note: A giant statue inside Mount Ida: gold head, silver arms, brass chest, iron below, one clay foot it leans on. Every part but the gold is cracked, and its tears become Acheron, Styx, Phlegethon and Cocytus.
Dante's old mentor, the scholar who wrote the Tesoretto. He prophesies Dante's fame and exile, then runs off like a winner of a footrace.
nodes.it: Siete voi qui, ser Brunetto?

nodes.n: Priscian, Francesco d'Accorso, Andrea de' Mozzi
nodes.note: Clerics and scholars in Brunetto's band.
Three honored Florentines circle like a wheel so they can keep their faces toward Dante while they talk.
The red stream drops over the great cliff with a roar like the falls at San Benedetto dell'Alpe.
Dante unties the cord around his waist, which he once meant to catch the leopard with. Virgil throws it into the abyss as a signal.
Each sits at the cliff's edge staring at a purse round his neck stamped with his family arms: Gianfigliazzi (blue lion on yellow), Ubriachi (white goose on red), Scrovegni (blue sow).
The image of fraud: the face of an honest man, a serpent's body, hairy paws, a scorpion's tail. He flies them down in wide, slow circles (XVII.115-117).
nodes.it: Ecco la fiera con la coda aguzza,
nodes.en: Behold the monster with the pointed tail,

nodes.note: Ten concentric ditches of iron-gray stone sloping to the central well, crossed by stone ridges like bridges from a castle's moats.
nodes.it: Luogo è in inferno detto Malebolge,
nodes.en: There is a place in Hell called Malebolge,

nodes.note: They whip two lines of sinners marching in opposite directions, like pilgrims crossing Rome's bridge in the Jubilee of 1300.
A Bolognese who sold his own sister to the lust of the Marquis of Este.
Still kingly. He seduced and abandoned Hypsipyle, then Medea.
A flatterer of Lucca, plunged in human excrement.
The courtesan from Terence's comedy, scratching herself with filthy nails.
Stuck head-first in round holes like baptismal fonts, soles of their feet burning. Dante mentions breaking one such font to save a drowning boy (XIX.16-21).
Mistakes Dante for Boniface VIII arriving early. Popes stack in the same hole; Boniface, then Clement V will push him down.
nodes.it: Se' tu già costì ritto, Bonifazio?
nodes.en: Dost thou stand there already, Boniface?

nodes.note: Still alive in 1300, so Dante can only place him in the future. He was pope when Dante was exiled.
Their heads face backward, so their tears run down their backs. Dante weeps; Virgil rebukes pity for the justly damned.
Manto leads to Virgil's long account of founding Mantua (XX.58-99).
Ancient and medieval astrologers and fortune-tellers.
Dark like the pitch boiling in Venice's Arsenal in winter to caulk ships.
A Lucca magistrate thrown in by a demon who says everyone in Lucca is a barrator.

The “Evil Claws”: Malacoda, Barbariccia, Alichino, Calcabrina, Cagnazzo, Libicocco, Draghignazzo, Ciriatto, Graffiacane, Farfarello, Rubicante, Scarmiglione. Malacoda lies that another bridge is still whole.
Malacoda says that yesterday, five hours later than now, it was 1,266 years since the bridges broke. Christ died at 34, so 34 + 1266 puts this on Holy Saturday morning, 1300.
Hooked out of the pitch, he tricks the demons and dives back in. Alichino and Calcabrina brawl and fall into the pitch.
Sardinian officials who sold favors. Michel Zanche's killer, Branca Doria, turns up in Ptolomea.
Slow processions in cloaks gilded outside and lead inside, cut like a monk's habit at Cluny.
“Jovial Friars” of Bologna who governed Florence together. Catalano reveals Malacoda lied: every bridge here is broken (XXIII.133-144).
The high priest who advised that one man die for the people, crucified on the ground for every hypocrite to walk over.
The ridges across bolgia 6 collapsed in the earthquake at Christ's death. They climb out on the rubble (XXIV.19-60).
Naked runners with hands tied behind by snakes. More kinds of serpent than all of Libya's sand.

Bitten, burns to ash and re-forms like the phoenix. He stole from a church in Pistoia, prophesies against Dante's party, then makes an obscene gesture at God. Dante says not even Capaneus was so proud (XXV.13-15).
A centaur covered in snakes with a fire-breathing dragon on his shoulders. Not with his brothers on the river of blood, because he stole Hercules' cattle by fraud.
Cianfa (a six-legged serpent) fuses with Agnello into one monster; Francesco Cavalcanti and Buoso swap shapes, man and snake. Puccio Sciancato alone stays unchanged.
Each flame hides a soul, like the fireflies a farmer sees down in the valley on a summer evening.
Shares a forked flame with Diomedes for the Trojan Horse and other tricks. Tells of his last voyage past Gibraltar, sunk within sight of a great mountain (Purgatory).
nodes.it: fatti non foste a viver come bruti, / ma per seguir virtute e canoscenza.
nodes.en: Ye were not made to live like unto brutes, / But for pursuit of virtue and of knowledge.

nodes.note: The other horn of the flame. Silent.
A warlord turned friar. Boniface VIII pre-absolved him for advising how to take Palestrina by false promises. St. Francis came for his soul; a black cherub won it.
Dante, writing in 14th-century Christian Europe, places them here as founders of a schism. A demon with a sword splits each sinner again on every lap.
Curio, who urged Caesar across the Rubicon, has his tongue cut out.
Both hands cut off. His advice (“a thing done has an end”) started the Guelph–Ghibelline feud in Florence. One of the five Ciacco named.
Carries his severed head like a lantern; he turned the Young King against his father Henry II. The poem's clearest statement of contrapasso.
nodes.it: Così s'osserva in me lo contrapasso.
nodes.en: Thus is observed in me the counterpoise.

nodes.note: Dante's father's cousin, murdered and never avenged. He points angrily at Dante and walks off.
Alchemists propped against each other, scratching scabs off like a knife scaling fish. The whole ditch is a plague hospital.
Impersonators running rabid. Schicchi posed as dead Buoso Donati to forge a will and won a prize mare.
Counterfeited Florentine gold florins. Swollen with dropsy, he dreams of the streams of the Casentino. He gives the bolgia's size (XXX.86-87).
Liars burning with fever. Sinon (who talked Troy into the horse) brawls with Master Adam.
Louder than the horn Roland blew at Roncesvalles.
Builder of Babel. His face is as long as St. Peter's bronze pinecone; he speaks a language no one understands.
nodes.it: Raphèl maì amècche zabì almi

nodes.note: Chained five times around; he fought the gods. Briareus is said to stand farther off.
Unchained because he did not fight the gods. He picks them up and sets them on the ice, bending like the leaning Garisenda tower in Bologna.
A lake frozen so hard it looks like glass; it would not crack if a mountain fell on it. Lucifer's wings keep it frozen (XXXIV.46-52).
Napoleone and Alessandro killed each other over their inheritance. Frozen face to face, butting like goats.
Mordred, whose chest Arthur pierced so light shone through. Camicion de' Pazzi waits for his kinsman Carlino to make him look better.
Betrayed the Florentine Guelphs at Montaperti. Dante kicks his face and pulls his hair; he names others: Buoso da Duera, Beccheria, Soldanieri, Ganelon, Tebaldello.
Gnaws Archbishop Ruggieri's skull. Sealed in a Pisan tower with his sons and grandsons, he watched them starve.
nodes.it: Poscia, più che 'l dolor, poté 'l digiuno.
nodes.en: Then hunger did what sorrow could not do.

nodes.note: Ugolino's betrayer, now his meal.
Had his guests murdered at dessert: “the fruit of the evil garden.” His soul fell here while a demon runs his still-living body on earth.
Murdered his father-in-law Michel Zanche at a banquet. Still walking around Genoa in 1300, but his soul has been here for years.
Faces turned up; their first tears freeze into crystal visors so grief turns back inside.
Completely covered, showing through like straw in glass: lying, standing, head-down, bent like bows.
Chest-deep in the ice. Three faces (red, yellow-white, black), six bat wings making the freezing wind, weeping from six eyes.
nodes.it: Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni / verso di noi; però dinanzi mira
nodes.en: Vexilla Regis prodeunt Inferni / Towards us; therefore look in front of thee

nodes.note: In the front mouth, head inside, legs kicking; his back flayed by claws.
Hangs from the black face, writhing without a word.
“Who looks so sturdy” in the third mouth.
At Lucifer's hip Virgil turns head-to-feet: they pass “the point to which all weights are drawn.” Down becomes up.
nodes.it: 'l punto / al qual si traggon d'ogne parte i pesi.

nodes.note: When he fell from heaven, the land fled from him to the north; the displaced earth rushed up to form the mountain of Purgatory.
Following a little stream up a hidden passage, they come out under the stars. Each of the three canticles ends on the word stelle.
nodes.it: E quindi uscimmo a riveder le stelle.
nodes.en: Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars.

edges.note: “Caina waits for him who quenched our life”: her husband Gianciotto
Christ broke the outer gate; it stays unlocked
The same quake broke the bridges of bolgia 6
Malacoda lied that another bridge was whole
The cord Dante meant to snare the leopard with
Thrown into the abyss, it summons Geryon
Nicholas expects Boniface to replace him in the hole
Minos wraps his tail eight times for Guido
One flame, split at the top
He drowned in sight of the mountain
Dante says not even Capaneus was this proud against God
A centaur kept apart from his brothers for fraud
Schicchi impersonated Buoso Donati; many commentators read the Buoso among the thieves as the same family
Virgil went down this far once before, summoned by the witch Erichtho
Beatrice came to Limbo to send Virgil
His fall pushed up the mountain
Celestine's resignation made way for Boniface

tableaux.note: Virgil throws the cord into the abyss as a signal; the poem states the throw, the timing against the journey bar is staging.
Geryon comes up out of the abyss, waits on the ledge, then carries them down in slow circles (XVII.115-117) to the first bolgia; the sequence is from the poem, the keyframes are staging.
The red stream drops over the great cliff into the eighth circle; the poem gives the fall and its roar, the width and mist are staging.
Two files of the pandering and seduced, walking in opposite directions along the ditch; the poem states the opposed directions, the pace and spacing are staging.
The opposite file, seen as 'coming toward us' in the poem.
Horned demons with great whips lash the walkers; where they stand is staging.
